result: The manuscript establishes the basic anatomy and function of the rat vibrissal system, describing how tactile information flows from whisker mechanoreceptors through the trigeminal ganglion to central brain structures.
evaluation: Claims C1, C4-C7 describe well-established neuroanatomy of the vibrissal system, supported by appropriate citations (Ebara et al., 2002; Jones et al., 2004a; Leiser and Moxon, 2006, 2007). This foundational knowledge provides context for the study.

result: Previous literature has predominantly characterized Vg neuron responses in terms of kinematic variables such as radial distance, angular position, and angular velocity.
evaluation: Claims C2, C8-C9, and C88 accurately characterize the existing literature with extensive citations. This establishes the historical context and motivation for investigating whether mechanical variables might provide better explanations.

result: Under standard experimental protocols using small angle deflections near the whisker base, kinematic and mechanical variables are tightly coupled, preventing discrimination between kinematic versus mechanical encoding.
evaluation: Claims C11-C13 and C90-C92 provide a logical inference about why previous studies could not distinguish between coding schemes. This is supported by citations to standard experimental practices and is consistent with the physics of whisker bending.

result: A novel manual stimulation technique was developed that allows large angle deflections far from the whisker base, systematically exploring regions of input space where kinematics and mechanics decouple.
evaluation: Claims C14-C15, C44-C46, C98-C100 describe the key methodological innovation. Figure 3 provides clear visual evidence that manual stimulation samples a larger, more decoupled input space compared to active whisking. This is a critical experimental advance.

result: In anesthetized rats, high-speed video (300 fps) was recorded during manual deflection of 18 whiskers while simultaneously recording from 22 Vg neurons, with deflections applied at variable radial distances up to 90% of whisker length.
evaluation: Claims C21-C28 and C178-C200 provide detailed experimental methodology for anesthetized recordings. The methods are clearly described with appropriate technical specifications. Sample sizes are modest but reasonable for single-unit recordings.

result: In awake rats, high-speed video (1000 fps) was recorded while seven whiskers contacted a vertical pole, with recordings from nine Vg neurons.
evaluation: Claims C36 and C201-C209 describe the awake recording methodology. The approach is well-documented, though the sample size for awake recordings is smaller (9 neurons vs 22 in anesthetized).

result: Kinematic variables (radial distance r, angular displacement θ, velocity V) were extracted from whisker shape tracked in video frames using the Whisk software.
evaluation: Claims C29-C31 and C210-C213 describe kinematic variable extraction with appropriate methodological detail and citation to the tracking software (Clack et al., 2012). The approach is standard for whisker tracking studies.

result: Mechanical variables (axial force Fx, transverse force Fy, bending moment M) were computed using a validated quasi-static model of whisker bending that accounts for full whisker shape.
evaluation: Claims C32, C34, C128-C130 describe the mechanical modeling approach with citations to validation studies (Birdwell et al., 2007; Solomon and Hartmann, 2008, 2010; Huet and Hartmann, 2016; Huet et al., 2015). This represents an advantage over simpler approximations.

result: Analyses were restricted to distal contacts (>40% whisker length) in anesthetized animals where the follicle does not move appreciably, as proximal contacts cause follicle translation and rotation.
evaluation: Claims C47-C55 address an important experimental consideration. Video 6 provides direct evidence of follicle movement during proximal contact. The restriction to distal contacts is justified, though it limits the generalizability of findings.

result: Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) with raised cosine basis functions covering 75 ms history were used to predict Vg firing rates, with 10-fold cross-validation to prevent overfitting.
evaluation: Claims C57-C63, C111-C113, C217-C219 describe the GLM methodology with appropriate citations (Pillow et al., 2008; Bale et al., 2013). The approach is standard for neural encoding studies and includes proper cross-validation.

result: GLM analysis revealed that the most recent time period (0-4 ms) is most important for predicting spikes, and bending moment M has the largest coefficients, indicating it is the most important predictor of firing activity on average.
evaluation: Claims C64-C68 and C102 are supported by Figure 4B showing coefficient magnitudes across neurons. The temporal weighting and importance of moment are clearly demonstrated in the data.

result: Subset model analysis shows an inverse relationship between mechanical and kinematic model predictions: when mechanical variables account well for full model predictions, kinematic variables do not, and vice versa.
evaluation: Claims C71-C74 and C103 are supported by Figure 5A-B showing specific examples and population data. The inverse relationship is clearly visible in Figure 5B, indicating that neurons rely primarily on one set of variables or the other.

result: The full GLM model achieved modest prediction accuracy with median R=0.30 (max=0.65), with no significant difference between active contact and passive deflections (p=0.18).
evaluation: Claims C75-C76 and C144-C145 report model performance metrics shown in Figure 6A. The authors acknowledge the modest performance and provide multiple explanations (2D analysis, quasi-static model limitations, temporal resolution constraints).

result: For manual stimulation, mechanical subset models performed significantly better than kinematic models (75% of neurons, p<0.05), but no preference was evident during active touch (p=0.43).
evaluation: Claims C77-C82 and C104-C106 present the key statistical findings shown in Figure 6B-C. The statistical tests are appropriate (Wilcoxon signed rank test, paired t-test) and support the main conclusion about mechanical encoding during decoupled stimulation.

result: During active touch, the input space is smaller and kinematics/mechanics remain coupled, explaining why mechanical models did not outperform kinematic models in awake animals.
evaluation: Claims C83-C84 and C107-C110 provide a logical explanation for the null result in awake animals, directly linking back to Figure 3 showing the coupled input space during active whisking. This interpretation is consistent with the study's framework.

result: The main finding is that Vg neurons more directly encode mechanical signals than kinematic signals when whiskers are deflected in a decoupled stimulus space, demonstrating that mechanics more accurately predict primary sensory neuron firing than kinematics within the hypothesis of linear-non-linear encoding.
evaluation: Claims C3, C20, C101, and C171 state the central conclusion, which is well-supported by the GLM analyses (Figures 4-6), the demonstration of decoupling (Figure 3), and appropriate statistical tests. The conclusion is appropriately qualified by the LNL encoding assumption.

result: The present work and Campagner et al. (2016) agree that Vg neurons encode mechanical variables more robustly than kinematic variables, with differences in findings explained by methodological variations in how kinematic variables were defined and mechanical variables were computed.
evaluation: Claims C93-C97, C121, C125-C127, and C131 provide a detailed comparison with Campagner et al. (2016). The authors correctly identify that apparent discrepancies arise from the use of θ_head versus θ_push and different mechanical modeling approaches.

result: The mechanical encoding framework provides a unified explanation for both phase tuning during non-contact whisking and responses during contact, with phase encoding potentially resulting from inertial forces during high angular acceleration.
evaluation: Claims C132-C141 propose an integrative hypothesis linking findings from multiple studies (Wallach et al., 2016; Campagner et al., 2016; Quist et al., 2014). While intellectually compelling, C136-C138 explicitly acknowledge this requires future verification with dynamic models. The hypothesis is speculative but well-reasoned.

result: R values were computed only during contact periods to avoid artificial inflation from correctly predicting zero activity during non-contact; including non-contact periods increased median R-values from 0.27 to 0.47 for kinematic models and 0.26 to 0.38 for mechanical models.
evaluation: Claims C146-C149 and C221-C223 explain an important methodological choice. The rationale is sound: any variable capturing contact/non-contact transitions would trivially predict firing changes. The alternative analysis (C147) demonstrates the magnitude of this effect.

result: The analysis is limited to 2D despite evidence that whiskers move in 3D and Vg neurons are directionally tuned in three dimensions.
evaluation: Claims C150-C152 acknowledge a significant limitation with appropriate citations. This is an honest assessment that 3D analysis would likely improve model performance but was not technically feasible in this study.

result: The quasi-static models omit friction and whisker dynamics (collisions, vibrations), and predicting spikes at high temporal resolution would require dynamic models and tracking beyond current videographic capabilities.
evaluation: Claims C153-C154 acknowledge important modeling limitations with citations. This is a fair assessment of what would be required for improved predictions, though it represents future work rather than a flaw in the current approach.

result: The GLM's linear-nonlinear framework with a single global nonlinearity may be too simplistic for the wide input space sampled, potentially explaining the relatively low prediction quality.
evaluation: Claims C155-C160 provide thoughtful speculation about model limitations. The authors correctly note that GLMs assume a single linearization across the full input space, which may not hold when sampling widely. This is honest self-criticism.

result: Temporal resolution was limited to 15 ms (versus 100 ms in Campagner et al. 2016), considerably less than the ms or sub-ms resolution of Vg neurons, due to experimental constraints in the temporal resolution of kinematic and mechanical variables.
evaluation: Claims C161-C163 acknowledge temporal resolution limitations with appropriate citations (Bale et al., 2015; Jones et al., 2004a). The comparison with Campagner et al. shows the present work actually achieved better temporal resolution despite limitations.

result: Single-trial modeling was used rather than trial averaging because precise stimulus duplication would require sampling a narrow input space, which was deliberately avoided to achieve kinematic-mechanical decoupling.
evaluation: Claims C164-C170 explain why trial averaging (which could improve predictions per Bale et al., 2013) was not used. The reasoning is sound: achieving decoupling required sampling broadly, which precluded precise stimulus replication.

result: A more stringent test would require full 3D characterization at higher spatiotemporal resolution, dynamic whisker models, and possibly more sophisticated modeling beyond GLMs; access to large, decoupled input spaces is critical for understanding Vg coding during natural behavior.
evaluation: Claims C172-C177 outline future directions with appropriate citations about natural whisking complexity. This provides a roadmap for advancing the field while acknowledging current limitations.
